newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts dismiss Swiss economic stimulus package.
newsitem.headline: Analysts dismiss Swiss economic stimulus package.

text.p: The Swiss government's plan to stimulate the stagnant economy primarily through extra infrastructure spending will do little to fuel growth or create many new jobs, analysts say.

The package, which parliament was widely expected to approve during a three-day special session in Berne that started on Monday, could even backfire by diverting attention from the real roots of Switzerland's economic woes, they say.

Swiss National Bank (SNB) Chairman Hans Meyer does not think much of the proposal, which includes 561 million Swiss francs in federal matching funds designed to spark a total of 2.4 billion in spending on infrastructure projects.

"It is hardly likely that the 500 million francs put in play by the government will contribute significantly to restarting growth," Meyer said in a speech last month, suggesting the money could be better spent in other ways.
Meyer has often stressed the importance of education and training and avoiding measures that boost the cost of labour as ways to bring down joblessness, which stands at 5.6 percent.

Goaded to act by six years of stagnation, the government hopes the scheme could add one third of a percentage point to gross domestic product (GDP) in 1998 and 1999. It says the 2.4 billion in envisioned spending could employ 24,000 people.

The focus will be on maintaining public infrastructure via construction of roads, tunnels and public buildings. It also includes funding for job training for young people and for refitting public and private buildings for energy efficiency.
Corporate tax reforms are also part of the package, but will not be voted on until June or later.
Thomas Schmidheiny, chief executive of building materials group Holderbank, has come out against the plan.
"This a political stunt. The construction sector really must redimension itself," he told a recent news conference.
"I do not believe we should pump oxygen into the system temporarily just to have the same problems later."

Franz Jaeger, director of St Gallen University's Institute for Empirical Economic Research, told the Finanz und Wirtschaft newspaper that Switzerland would be better served by stabilising its public finances.
Growing deficits pushed the public-sector shortfall to some 2.3 percent percent of GDP last year. Public-sector debt stood at 49.1 percent of GDP, according to provisional figures.

Stable finances would not just help Switzerland as a business centre, but also improve expectations for future income, which in turn helps fuel consumer confidence and encourage producers and investors to create jobs, Jaeger said.
He added it was far from sure that deficit-plagued cantons and local governments would make use of the plan or that many new jobs could be added amid excess capacity already on hand.
The plan could actually have an adverse effect if people saved more and spent less in the expectation that public deficits would widen and lead to higher taxes, he wrote.

"The longer we wait to make structural adjustments, break up cartels and weed out market-protecting rules designed to secure jobs," he added, "the more painful the losses of job security, growth and attractiveness as a place to do business will be."
Even the plan's proponents damn it with faint praise.

"The package is unspectacular, but within the realm of what can be done politically," Peter Tschopp, a member of parliament from Geneva, told the Handelszeitung newspaper. "It would also be insane to wait until we have a quarter million jobless."
